          "h": "The theme: The stubbornness of Israel versus the obstinacy of Pharaoh, and the reading of Parashat HaChodesh. When Israel prays \"Turn us unto You and we shall return,\" we plead: even though salvation begins with an awakening from Above (isarusa d'le'eila), once You turn us we will run after You, unlike the nations who rejected the Torah. Egypt worshipped the ram because it embodied the unholy Yesod—rigid stubbornness (akshanus). Israel is called \"stiff-necked\" (am kesheh oref, Shemos 32:9), but their stubbornness is holy: \"either a Jew or crucified\" (Shemos Rabbah 42:9), yet toward Hashem they are easily enticed to return. While Rabbi Eliezer held that the redemption will occur in Tishrei (dependent on human repentance), Rabbi Yehoshua held that it will occur in Nissan (sparked by divine grace, preceded by the harsh decrees of a king like Haman in Adar). On Rosh Chodesh Nissan, the portion of HaChodesh is read; eating the Korban Pesach internalizes the humility of the sheep, and sprinkling the blood surrenders the animal soul (nefesh ha-bahamis) to Hashem. Pharaoh (\"ha-oref\", the stiff neck) stood upon the Nile (Bereishis 41:1), attempting through sorcery to compel supernal forces to submit to his desires; the righteous, by contrast, place themselves beneath Hashem (\"and behold, Hashem stood above him\", Bereishis 28:13). Reading Parashat HaChodesh draws down the illumination of the final letter Hei, advancing the redemption from potentiality into actuality."

          "h": "The theme: The four New Years corresponding to the four letters of the Divine Name Ehyeh (אהי״ה) and the revelation of divine foreknowledge (Yedi'ah) versus free choice (Bechirah). The four New Years enumerated at the start of tractate Rosh Hashanah parallel the four letters of the Name Ehyeh—the name of Keser—through which the Exodus from Egypt was initiated (\"And they shall say to me: What is His name? ... Ehyeh has sent me unto you\", Shemos 3:13–14). The Exodus was the primal inception of all future redemptions, leaving the full stature of the cosmos to unfold across history. To Moshe alone was the phrase Asher Ehyeh (\"I shall be that I shall be\") revealed, alluding to the future subjugations of exile (Berachos 9b) because ongoing purifications were necessary; yet to the people Moshe was commanded to say merely \"Ehyeh has sent me,\" following the principle \"sufficient unto the hour is the affliction.\" As explained in Zohar Chadash and the Ari's Arba Me'ot Shekel Kesef, Yedi'ah and Bechirah reside in two separate spiritual dimensions: in the realm of Foreknowledge there is no free choice, a reality concealed in this world but destined to be unveiled in the Future when the yetzer is destroyed and the days arrive in which \"I have no pleasure\" (Shabbos 151b). Moshe, embodying Da'as, grasped this hidden realm where the heart's secret will binds with the intellect (liba l'fuma lo galya), bridging the lower letter Hei (speech / Knesset Israel) with the higher letter Hei (heart / Binah)."

        {
          "h": "The theme: Moshe at the Burning Bush, the three crowns (Torah, Priesthood, Royalty), and the three spiritual rungs of Ani, Attah, and Hu (אני, אתה, הוא). When Hashem first revealed Himself at the burning bush, Moshe declared \"Here am I\" (Hineni), sensing his readiness for both Priesthood and Kingship (Shemos Rabbah 2:6). Yet Hashem commanded \"Draw not near hither,\" revealing that the final purification had not yet arrived. The temporary perfection Israel tasted at Sinai was authentic for that hour, and through the purifications of exile they will regain those crowns, as expounded on \"and everlasting joy upon their heads\" (Yeshayah 35:10; Shabbat 88a). The three crowns—Torah, Kehunah, and Malchus (Avos 4:13)—correspond to the three grammatical and mystical pronouns: Ani [I], Attah [You], and Hu [He]. Ani corresponds to Malchus (\"and I am prayer\", Tehillim 109:4), the indwelling of the divine presence within the hearts of Israel. Attah corresponds to Priesthood (Kehunah): direct visual encounter with the Sovereign (\"You are a priest forever\", Tehillim 110:4), standing as a servant before the King, reflecting the golden frontplate (Tzitz, from hatzatzah, gazing) upon Aharon's forehead bearing the Name Havayah, and embodying Yitzchak Avinu who saw Hashem before him (\"I have set Hashem always before me\", Tehillim 16:8)."

Subtract twelve and a half years during which one prays and eats and uses the bathroom, and twelve and a half years remain for them. If You can endure them all and forgive the sins committed during those years, excellent. And if not, half of the sins are upon me to bear and half upon You. And if You say that all of them, the sins of all twelve and a half years that remain, are upon me, I sacrificed my soul before You and You should forgive them due to my merit.…’"

          "h": "The theme: The Crown of Torah as Hu [He], the mystery of \"I am He and no other\" (Ani Hu v'lo acheir), and the conduits of children, life, and sustenance (banei, chayei, u-mezonei). The Crown of Torah is the supreme rung of Hu [He], the transcendent hidden realm cleaved to Israel alone, whence supernal Chochmah emerges from Ayin [Nothingness]. The Torah in this world represents the \"fallen fruit\" (novelot) of supernal wisdom (Bereishis Rabbah 17:5), wherein absolute Foreknowledge is clothed in human free choice. On the first night of Pesach, Hashem revealed: \"I am He and no other\" (Ani Hu v'lo acheir)—uniting the lowest manifestation of the Shechinah (Ani / Malchus) with the most transcendent hidden light (Hu / Keser), empowering Israel to merit the Crown of Torah. At the Exodus, when Israel lay in spiritual degradation, Hashem created a \"pure heart\" ex nihilo (yesh me-ayin) out of the transcendent source called Ayin (the Mazal of Israel), from which stream children, life, and sustenance (banei, chayei, u-mezonei, Moed Katan 28a). Sustenance (mezonei) corresponds to the Table of Kings (Keser Malchus); Children (banei) corresponds to the Altar (Keser Kehunah), bringing peace between husband and wife through the Priesthood (the Sotah water restoring the letters of the Divine Name in procreation); Life (chayei) corresponds to the Torah, the Tree of Life (Keser Torah), the Central Pillar that binds all existence to the supernal Keser."

          "h": "The theme: The primordial depth revealed on the first day of Pesach, the name of Mashiach, and the three supernal crowns. On the first day of Pesach—the head of all festivals and the inception of Israel's national existence—the primordial depth of Keser was unveiled. In reward for this revelation, Israel will merit the name of Mashiach, which embodies the root holiness of the nation destined to endure forever (\"the lip of truth shall be established forever\", Mishlei 12:19). This reflects \"their beginning is wedged in their end\" (ne'utzan techilasan b'sofam): \"The first unto Zion: Behold, behold them\" (Yeshayah 41:27)—\"Zion\" denoting the gates distinguished in Halachah (Berachos 8a), and \"the first\" denoting the Crown of Torah (Keser Elyon), embracing the souls of Israel who arose in divine thought at the inception of Creation. Through ongoing remembrance of the Exodus in every generation, this light gradually emerges from concealment into full manifestation, culminating in the Resurrection of the Dead on Pesach. While the first day of Succos represents Yaakov journeying to Succos (the mystery of the Name Havayah and the rebuilding of the Temple / Avodah), and the taking of the Lulav accomplishes the subjugation of Esav (the first of the nations) and Gog (the last of the nations) through the elevation of Malchus (Ani), all three crowns were rooted simultaneously on Pesach through the transcendent name Ehyeh. Six months prior to the Exodus (in Tishrei) forced labor ceased, and twelve months prior (in Nissan) the first tidings arrived, awakening the spark of faith in the Name Ehyeh (I will be), advancing in Tishrei to the present liberation of the Name Havayah, and culminating on the night of the Exodus in the great awe of the revealed Shechinah: \"I am Hashem—I am He and no other.\""

          "h": "The theme: The letters of Ehyeh (אהי״ה), the Crown of a Good Name (Keser Shem Tov), and the essence of Yosef and Yehudah. The three crowns correspond to the three distinct letters Aleph-Yud-Hei of the Name Ehyeh: the Aleph is the transcendent head of all; the Yud is the inception of actualized perception ex nihilo, which expands into the letter Vav of the Name Havayah (the Central Pillar / Crown of Torah); the lower Hei is the crown of the final Hei of Havayah (Crown of Royalty). The first letter Hei of Ehyeh crowns the first Hei of Havayah, representing the Crown of a Good Name (Keser Shem Tov) which ascends above all three (Avos 4:13; Koheles 7:1). A \"good name\" is not a separate entity, but describes one who excels in Torah, Avodah, or Gemilus Chasadim—the three pillars of the world, which unite in the foundation of the single pillar called Tzaddik (Chagigah 12b; Mishlei 10:25). Israel is called \"the remnant of Yosef,\" embodying the consummate tzaddik who strictly adheres to the halachah; yet human exertion alone cannot escape all blemish (\"there is not a righteous man upon earth that does good and sins not\", Koheles 7:20). When Yosef brought an evil report against his brothers, he evaluated them from the standard of the consummate tzaddik. In truth, Israel is named after Yehudah—whose name spells the Tetragrammaton with the letter Dalet (דלות, spiritual poverty). Originally a Dalet, the soul recognizes its absolute deficiency and receives the divine seed from Above, expanding the Dalet into the fertile letter Hei, achieving the perfection of Knesset Israel."

        {
          "h": "The theme: The superiority of the penitent over the wholly righteous (ba'alei teshuvah over tzaddikim) and the crown of an everlasting name (shem olam). The ultimate cleaving will be realized when Israel is called by the Name of the Holy One (Bava Batra 75b) through Mashiach ben David from the seed of Yehudah. This is achieved through repentance, where the penitent ascends above the wholly righteous (Berachos 34b) into the transcendent realm of divine Foreknowledge (Yedi'ah) above free choice, where all past sins are rectified and transformed into merits. While the wholly righteous man operates within strict boundaries (hagdara) like precious oil fragrant only from chamber to hall (Koheles Rabbah 7:1), the penitent shatters all boundaries, acquiring his world in a single moment like Elazar ben Dordaya (Avodah Zarah 17a). This is the \"good name\" whose fragrance spreads from one end of the world to the other (Yevamos 16a), fulfilling: \"and he smelled the fragrance of his garments\" (Bereishis 27:27)—which Chazal read as \"the fragrance of his traitors\" (bogdav, Sanhedrin 37a), the sublime fragrance of sinners who repented. Consummate tzaddikim secure a lasting name through their physical children (shem olam d'Yosef / she'eirit Yosef); but the penitent, from within the brokenness of his heart (\"Hashem is near unto them that are of a broken heart\", Tehillim 34:19), merits an everlasting name (shem olam) directly within Hashem's house (Yeshayah 56:5). Even when darkness strikes the righteous (like David with Batsheva, arranged by Hashem to establish the yoke of repentance, Avodah Zarah 5a), it serves to reveal the divine light. At the final judgment, the righteous weep because they mistakenly thought their triumph over the yetzer had been achieved through their own strength; only then do they recognize that without divine aid they could never have conquered that mountain, arriving at the truth of the place where penitents stand."

        {
          "h": "The theme: Relying on one's own merit versus divine attribution, the Crown of a Good Name (Keser Shem Tov), and repentance through the first letter Hei. \"Whoever hangs his deliverance upon his own merit, Heaven hangs it upon the merit of others\" (Berachos 10b): when a person attributes spiritual attainment to his own striving, he remains separate from Hashem, so Heaven shows him that all is from Him; but when he nullifies himself and acknowledges that everything is from Hashem, Hashem attributes everything to him (\"the earth He has given to the children of men\", Tehillim 115:16). At the final judgment, the yetzer appears to the wicked as fine as a strand of hair (Sukkah 52a), and they weep because it was within their grasp to conquer it. The penitent who attains this brokenhearted weeping in his lifetime achieves the Crown of a Good Name (Keser Shem Tov) which transcends all crowns, issuing light directly out of darkness. While Hashem originally made man upright, desiring that no one ever sin in deed—content with the minimal darkness of the Serpent's mental incitement—once Adam sinned, the path of the Tree of Life (the unblemished tzaddik who never sins, like Eliyahu) was concealed. Thenceforth, the only path to eternal life is repentance (u'v'atah pen yishlach yado—\"now\" meaning repentance, Bereishis Rabbah 21:6), entering through the first letter Hei of the Name Havayah, where Hashem crowns him with the Crown of a Good Name hinted in the first Hei of Ehyeh."

And anyone who modestly bases his prayer or request upon the merit of others, when God answers his prayer, it is based upon his own merit. The Gemara cites proof from Moses. When he prayed to God for forgiveness after the incident of the Golden Calf, he based his request upon the merit of others, as it is stated: “Remember Abraham, Isaac and Israel your servants, to whom You swore upon Yourself, and told them: I will increase your descendants like the stars of the heavens, and all of this land of which I have spoken, I will give to your descendants and they will inherit it forever” (Exodus 32:13).…’",

          "h": "The theme: The four New Years, the four soul-powers, the four cosmic elements, and the rectification of dust (afar) and iron (barzel). At the Exodus, Israel merited the illumination of all four crowns embedded in Nissan, the head of all months. In their expansion, they branch into the four New Years: Nissan, Tishrei, Elul, and Shevat (Rosh Hashanah 2a). These correspond to the four soul faculties (Nefesh, Ruach, Neshamah, and Neshama le-Neshama / Chayah-Yechidah), parallel to the four bodily elements (fire, air, water, earth) and the four kingdoms of creation (inanimate, vegetative, animal, speaking). Earth (afar) encompasses all (\"all were of the dust\", Koheles 3:20; Koheles Rabbah 3:20—even the solar orb), and \"all return to dust\" is the mystery of repentance returning to the Source. On the first of Tishrei—the New Year for Shemitah and Yovel—holiness is infused into the earth and mineral kingdom through the penitent who humbles himself until his soul is as dust to all (v'nafshi ke-afar la-kol tihyeh). While the Serpent was cursed with eating dust (Bereishis 3:14), and iron (barzel) forms the harsh wall of exile and the sword of Esav (Berachos 32b), David HaMelech raised the yoke of repentance to turn the rejected stone into the head cornerstone (Tehillim 118:22). Mystically, BARZEL (בַּרְזֶל) forms the acronym of the four Matriarchs who built the House of Israel: Bilhah, Rachel, Zilpah, Leah (בלהה, רחל, זלפה, לאה); together with Yaakov (copper / nechoshes), they form the protective footwear of Knesset Israel: \"Iron and brass shall be your shoes\" (Devarim 33:25)."

          "h": "The theme: The Shofar of Rosh Hashanah, the Ten Days of Repentance, the Crown of Royalty (Keser Malchus), and the soul of David in Sodom. On Rosh Hashanah—\"the day of the conception of the world\" (Yom harat olam)—the souls of Israel who arose in primordial thought ascend to their Source through the simple sound of the Shofar (kol pashut), which precedes the articulation of verbal letters (the 22 letters of Creation). Moshe prayed: \"Hear, Hashem, the voice of Judah\" (Devarim 33:7), that Yehudah's voice of repentance merge into the primal \"voice of Jacob\" (Bereishis 27:22). Through the Shofar, the divine ascends from judgment to mercy (\"God ascends with a blast, Hashem with the sound of the shofar\", Tehillim 47:6), inaugurating the Ten Days of Repentance that culminate on Yom Kippur in the gate of freedom (tar'a d'cheiru / the higher Hei of Binah). The final Hei of Ehyeh crowns the final Hei of Havayah (Malchus), rectifying the primeval chaos (tohu) when the world was entirely water. Water fosters physical lust, the sin of the generation of the Flood; rectified, water becomes the lovingkindness of Avraham (\"the desire of a man is his kindness\", Mishlei 19:22). In pagan kings, monarchic power fosters unbridled physical lust; in Jewish kings, royalty requires absolute awe (\"once a king bows, he does not straighten\", Berachos 34b). Rava challenged Bar Sheshach (Avodah Zarah 65a): \"You fear a mortal king who restrains your pleasure, whereas Israel's fear of Hashem is their very desire!\" The Midrash asks: \"Where did I find David My servant? In Sodom!\" (Bereishis Rabbah 41:4)—the very crucible of depravity, whose fire incinerated evil through the fear of Yitzchak. Lot was rescued through the soul of David and the spirit of Mashiach which \"hovered over the face of the waters\" (Bereishis 1:2; Bereishis Rabbah 2:4)—the Crown of holy Royalty that hovers over all desires, touching yet not touching (noge'a v'eino noge'a), to elevate them into the Sanctuary."

          "h": "The theme: The holy root of Shevat, the tribe of Asher, the New Year for Trees, and the rectification of the covenant. The final letter Hei of the Name Havayah embodies the feminine principle (sod ha-nukva), the \"wisdom of women\" (chochmas nashim) that channels intense passion into holy awe (\"a woman that fears Hashem\", Mishlei 31:30). The Serpent instigated woman because within her resides the root of the \"lower waters\" (mayin nukvin) that weep to draw near unto the King, reflecting Israel’s yearning for Hashem (\"the desire of a woman is to her husband; the desire of Israel is to the Holy One\", Bereishis Rabbah 20:7). This quality spreads through the tribe of Asher (\"for the daughters will call me blessed [ishruni]\", Bereishis 30:13; \"blessed be Asher above sons\", Devarim 33:24), whose daughters were beautiful and married kings and High Priests (Bereishis Rabbah 71:10; 99:12), from whose maternal line Mashiach is destined to descend. In the order of the tribal princes in Nissan, Asher corresponds to the month of Shevat—the New Year for Trees (Rosh Hashanah 2a). By the fifteenth of Shevat most of the year's rains have fallen (Rosh Hashanah 14a); descending upper waters evoke ascending lower waters, enabling trees to blossom and bear fruit. Physical fruitfulness derives from the sanctified drive of passion (ko'ach ha-ta'avah bi-kdushah, Yoma 69b); the vegetative soul (nefesh ha-tzomachat) from the element of water generates the righteous offspring of Israel (\"seed for you to sow\", Bereishis 47:23). Shevat is the crown and root of this power, paralleling the final Hei of Ehyeh, making it the prime season during the weeks of Shovavim to rectify nocturnal emissions and wasted seed. Because the unholy shell mirrors the holy (zeh l'umas zeh), Asher's territory was most vulnerable to involuntary emissions; Amos, descended from Asher, challenged: \"Are you not as children of the Ethiopians unto Me?\" (Amos 9:7), culminating in \"the treader of grapes with him that draws forth the seed\" (ibid. 9:13). Overcoming this deficiency rectifies the Nefesh. In contrast, rectifying the Ruach occurs in Elul through the letter Vav (the element of air/spirit) and its crown Yud of Ehyeh, celebrated on the first of Elul as the New Year for animal tithing (ma'asar behemah), rectifying the animal spirit (ruach ha-behemah) through the prince of Gad in preparation for Tishrei."

          "h": "The theme: The curse of Gad (arur shocheiv im kol behemah), the kelipah of the dog, and Eliyahu subverting pagan desire into Torah. Among the eleven curses of Mount Ebal (Devarim 27), \"Cursed be he that lies with any manner of beast\" corresponds to Gad, following the authority in Kilayim (8:6) that a dog is halachically categorized as a beast (kelev min behemah). The Talmud notes that the Torah is beloved to Israel as a queen (shegal) is to the nations (Rosh Hashanah 4a), comparing gentile lust to a female dog because a dog remains locked during coitus (Sanhedrin 108b); so too, the Aramite woman is bound to her paramour like a dog (Tanchuma, Vayeshev 3). The nations are chained to physical lust; Israel’s lust is bound to the Torah, for illicit passion exists only in a heart empty of Torah (Rambam, Issurei Biah 22:21; Kiddushin 30b). In the unholy realm, this animal passion is the shell of the dog (\"Deliver my soul from the sword, my only one from the power of the dog\", Tehillim 22:21). The dog is the most promiscuous of beasts, mating even aboard Noach's Ark (Sanhedrin 108b); the numerical value of Behemah (בְּהֵמָה = 52) equals Kelev (כֶּלֶב = 52). The Midrash expounds \"Gad comes\" (ba Gad, Bereishis 30:11) as \"he who cuts down (goded) the foundation of the nations\" (Bereishis Rabbah 71:9)—namely shattering their unholy lust. This was accomplished by the prophet Eliyahu from the tribe of Gad (Shir HaShirim Rabbah 2:5), who embodies the antithesis of animal lust and therefore lives forever (chai l'olam). Physical death stems from the Serpent casting defilement into Chavah (Shabbat 146a); Israel channels desire into the Torah of eternal life. Pinchas—who is Eliyahu (Bava Metzia 114b)—displayed holy zealotry against Zimri and Cozbi, meriting the Crown of Priesthood (Keser Kehunah) which guards Israel's genealogical purity (Kesubos 13a). The High Priest is sequestered seven days before Yom Kippur (Yoma 2a) to atone for the fallen angels Uzza and Azael (Yoma 67b), and before burning the Red Heifer to cleanse the taint of death, attaining the purity of an angel (mal'ach)."

          "h": "The theme: Pinchas/Eliyahu as the Angel of the Covenant and the salvation of the Jewish soul from Gehinnom. Eliyahu became a complete angel (mal'ach), and initially Pinchas was likewise an angel whom Rachav did not need to hide (Tanchuma, Pinchas 1), expounded on \"And an angel of Hashem came up from Gilgal\" (Shoftim 2:1)—this was Pinchas. He is designated the \"Angel of the Covenant\" (Mal'ach HaBris, Malachi 3:1), for whom a chair is set at every circumcision, demarcating the boundary between Israel and the nations regarding sexual desire. Spiritual foreskin (orlah) applies only to the nations: even when gentiles practice physical circumcision (Nedarim 31b), their root remains embedded in lust; conversely, even an uncircumcised Jew is called circumcised (mahul b'kho'ach) because at his ancestral root he is circumcised. Therefore, Avraham Avinu—the head of the circumcised—sits at the entrance of Gehinnom to extract every circumcised Jew from punishment (Eruvin 19a), the covenant of circumcision testifying on their behalf that their sins were merely like external thorns around the myrtle (asa d'kayei beinei hotzei). The sole exception is one who cohabited with an Aramite woman (bo'el aramiss), whose foreskin is drawn down (mimshecha orlasei) so that Avraham does not recognize him. Yet even the person with a drawn foreskin (mashuch) is biblically circumcised, his defect being merely outward to human eyes; Hashem Himself, Who looks into the heart (I Shmuel 16:7), rescues him, seeing that in the depths of his soul he remains circumcised. Pinchas/Eliyahu became zealous over this sin, turning into an angel who perceives the inner thoughts of man (Tosafos, Shabbat 12b), seeing with the heavenly court (Hu u-veit dino) that even the fallen Jew remains pure in the inner depths of his heart."

          "h": "The theme: The revelation of Eliyahu, the purification of desire, the mystery of the End of Days (Keitz), and the name of Eliyahu. The revelation of Eliyahu (Gilui Eliyahu) is granted to one whose inward heart is illuminated by Hashem in purity from every trace of lust. Prior to the great and terrible day of Hashem, Eliyahu is sent to purify the hearts of Israel from all evil desires at their very root, leading directly to the Resurrection of the Dead (Sotah 49b) and turning the heart of the fathers to the children (Eduyot 8:7; Malachi 3:24). The Patriarchs rectified the sin of Adam HaRishon in their own personal root, but in their descendants this rectification remains incomplete until the Keitz—which Yaakov Avinu sought to reveal to his sons (Bereishis 49:1; Pesachim 56a), but which was closed to him because the Keitz belongs to divine Foreknowledge (Yedi'ah) while human history is governed by free choice (Bechirah). The Tetragrammaton with its feminine filling (milui ha-nukva) has the numerical value of Ban (ב״ן = 52), reflecting \"You are children (banim) unto Hashem your God\" (Devarim 14:1) and the holy feminine waters (mayin nukvin). The nations, who are not called Adam (Yevamos 61a) but Behemah (בְּהֵמָה = 52), channel this into carnal lust; Israel, called Adam (אָדָם = 45 / מ״ה), channel it into the masculine world of Mah (עולם התיקון). Eliyahu equals 52 (Ban / ב״ן) and in small gematria 16 (יו״ד-וָי״ו), uniting the Yud of Ehyeh with the Vav of Havayah—the \"true sign\" (os emes) that Rachav sought when converting (Zohar III, 2a). Coitus with an Aramite woman severs one from this holy covenant, plunging the soul into the unholy shell of the dog (כֶּלֶב = 52). David feared this after marrying the captive woman (yefat to'ar, Sanhedrin 107a), which bore Avshalom, crying: \"Deliver my soul from the sword, my only one from the power of the dog\" (Tehillim 22:21). Rachav converted and married Yehoshua, producing prophets and priests; Eliyahu unites both as the prophet-priest who resolves all halachic doubts (Teiku) and will restore the Kohanim to their service using the ashes of the Red Heifer."

          "h": "The theme: \"The fortune of the world has come\" (Ba gada d'alma), the elevation of the animal soul (Nefesh HaBahamis), and the trial of Yehoshua ben Yehotzadak. The Midrash expounds \"Gad comes\" (ba Gad, Bereishis 30:11) as ba gada d'alma—the fortune of the entire world has arrived (Bereishis Rabbah 71:9). Israel is called Adam and possesses a transcendent destiny (mazal) originating from Ayin [Keser] (Bava Kamma 2b), whereas beasts have no such destiny. Through Eliyahu, who turns the heart of children to fathers, the whole world is unified at its Source; even the animal soul (nefesh ha-bahamis) is elevated through its inclusion within the human soul. Eliyahu equals Behemah (52 / בְּהֵמָה), holding fast to the letter Vav that extends to the Yud, fulfilling \"Man and beast You save, Hashem\" (Tehillim 36:7)—referring to humble Israelites who make themselves like beasts before Hashem (\"I was as a beast before You\", Tehillim 73:22; Chullin 5b). David HaMelech elevates even the unlearned masses (amei ha-aretz, termed \"the beasts within you\", Bereishis Rabbah 41:4). In the era of the Second Temple, Israel was worthy of miracles as in the days of Yehoshua bin Nun (Berachos 4a), but this was aborted because the people married foreign women, producing the soiled garments of the High Priest Yehoshua ben Yehotzadak (Zechariah 3:3; Sanhedrin 93a). When the false prophets Ahab and Zedekiah were cast into the fiery furnace of Babylon for adulterous designs, they demanded Yehoshua ben Yehotzadak enter with them, hoping his righteousness would save them. Yehoshua was saved while they were incinerated; yet his garments were singed (icharach manei) because his descendants married non-Jewish women. In the upper world, the angel immediately stripped away the soiled garments and clothed him in robes of state (machalatzos), but the ultimate Keitz was postponed, prophecy departed, and the Shechinah did not reside in the Second Temple (Yoma 21b) because the Shechinah dwells only among genealogically unmixed families (Kiddushin 70b), a purity restored by Ezra and to be consummated by Eliyahu."

        {
          "h": "The theme: The sanctity of genealogical lineage (Yichus), \"The fortune of the house\" (Gada d'veisa), and the rectification of the month of Elul. The supreme virtue of Israel is their genealogical purity: \"Bring me the book of genealogies as my children bring\" (Bamidbar Rabbah 9:7). Pagan nations, compared to donkeys, possess no paternal lineage (ein av l'akum, Yevamos 98a), being like animals. In Jacob's blessing: \"Gad, a troop shall march on his heels\" (Gad gedud yegudenu, Bereishis 49:19)—those who went forth in the armies of the House of David were certified of pure lineage (Kiddushin 76b). \"Gad comes\" (ba Gad, Bereishis 30:11) means gada d'veisa—the fortune of the house, for true good fortune (mazal tov) is holy lineage. Lineage is the transcendent Ayin from which the Yesh [children] is hewn; when a child is born or one marries, we wish Mazal Tov because the family house (Beis Aharon, Beis David) is built. The order of rectification begins with one's house (gada d'veisa), expands to the community (gada d'alma), and culminates in shattering the foundations of the nations who seek to mix human seed with the beast. In the sacred calendar, the time for rectifying this beast-like desire is the month of Elul, when we infuse holiness into animals through animal tithing (ma'asar behemah)."

          "h": "The theme: The timing of the Redemption in Tishrei (\"I will hasten it\" / Achishenah) versus Nissan (\"in its time\" / B'itah), and the revelation of the Wonder (Pele). If Israel merits redemption through their own repentance from below, all agree it will unfold in Tishrei (according to Rabbi Eliezer, Rosh Hashanah 11a) on Rosh Hashanah itself, preceded by the arrival of Eliyahu on 29 Elul (since the restriction against Eliyahu arriving on the eve of a festival due to festival preparation does not apply to Rosh Hashanah, where some even fast). Elul is thus perpetually primed for the revelation of Eliyahu. Conversely, if redemption comes without prior merit—\"in its time\" (b'itah, Sanhedrin 98a)—it will occur in Nissan (according to Rabbi Yehoshua), mirroring the Exodus where Hashem extracted \"a nation from the midst of another nation\" (Devarim 4:34). In Nissan, redemption will begin on Rosh Chodesh Nissan (since Mashiach does not arrive on Yom Tov itself, Eruvin 43b), the day that took ten crowns (Shabbat 87b) representing the Crown of Torah (Keser Torah). The Torah of this world is mere vanity compared to the Torah of Mashiach (Koheles Rabbah 11:8), like steam rising from a cooking pot compared to the concentrated essence within. Then the supernal wonder (Pele) will be revealed: Hashem performing miracles for those who appear unworthy. Israel, rooted in primordial divine thought, grasps this Pele—the letter Aleph of Ehyeh—which rectifies the articulate soul (nefesh ha-medaberes) and elevates speech from the exile of Egypt into holy revelation."

In the verse: “I the Lord in its time I will hasten it” (Isaiah 60:22), it is written: “In its time,” indicating that there is a designated time for the redemption, and it is written: “I will hasten it,” indicating that there is no set time for the redemption.                       "text": ": ‘§ Rabbi Alexandri says: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi raises a contradiction in a verse addressing God’s commitment to redeem the Jewish people. In the verse: “I the Lord in its time I will hasten it” (Isaiah 60:22), it is written: “In its time,” indicating that there is a designated time for the redemption, and it is written: “I will hasten it,” indicating that there is no set time for the redemption. Rabbi Alexandri explains: If they merit redemption through repentance and good deeds I will hasten the coming of the Messiah. If they do not merit redemption, the coming of the Messiah will be in its designated time.’"

        {
          "h": "The theme: The opening letter Aleph of Anochi, the two crowns of Sinai, and the distinction between \"I will show you\" (ar'echa) and \"I will show him\" (ar'enu). The Decalogue opens with the letter Aleph of Anochi (Shemos 20:2), welling from the primordial depth of speech; thence Israel merited the two crowns of Na'aseh and Nishma—the Crown of Torah and the Crown of Priesthood (which was shared by all Israel before being given specifically to Aharon, when they were called a \"kingdom of priests\", Shemos 19:6). At Sinai this was an open revelation, whereas at the Exodus it was hidden, Hashem communicating to Moshe: \"when you have brought forth the people out of Egypt, you shall serve God upon this mountain\" (Shemos 3:12). The name Ehyeh signifies the future: \"I will be with them.\" In Nissan this initial light is unveiled, being the New Year for kings and festivals (Rosh Hashanah 2a), sanctifying the articulate soul (medaber) just as the other three New Years sanctify the mineral, vegetative, and animal realms. In the future redemption, Scripture declares: \"According to the days of your coming out of the land of Egypt will I show him marvelous things (ar'enu nifla'ot)\" (Michah 7:15). Regarding the Exodus it says \"your coming out\" in the second person (tzascha), because every Jew in every generation experiences and perceives the Exodus; but regarding the future redemption without merit (b'itah), Scripture shifts to the third person: \"I will show him (ar'enu),\" because that sudden, unearned supernatural light cannot be comprehended in this world prior to its actual historical arrival."

        {
          "h": "The theme: The prospective illumination of time, the superiority of Rosh Chodesh in the Future, and the four stations of the Name Ehyeh across Nissan. Just as in the attribute of punishment a plague strikes both in front and behind (\"and pursued as far as Dan\", Bereishis 14:14; Bereishis Rabbah 43:2), how much more so in the abundant attribute of goodness: a sacred time sanctifies not only subsequent generations, but casts its radiant light beforehand into the day prepared for it. Thus, the light of the future redemption shines beforehand on Rosh Chodesh Nissan in every generation, especially in the footsteps of the Messiah (ikvesa d'Meshicha). In the Future, \"from one new moon to another, and from one sabbath to another\" (Yeshayah 66:23), Rosh Chodesh precedes Shabbat, its holiness surpassing that of Shabbat because human sanctification (Yisrael mekadshei l'zmanei) transformed into an eternal reality exceeds intrinsic, static sanctity. All four letters of the Name Ehyeh shine across Nissan: the Aleph on Rosh Chodesh; the first Hei on the tenth of Nissan (\"draw out and take you a lamb\", Shemos 12:21; Shemos Rabbah 16:2); the Vav (the crown of Keser) at the midnight Exodus on the fifteenth; and the final Hei on the Seventh Day of Pesach at the Splitting of the Sea, where water (passion) was transformed into a protective wall, empowering a simple handmaid to see what Yechezkel did not see. By observing these four stations in Nissan each year, Israel draws down this light, steadily hastening the End when all flesh shall see that the mouth of Hashem has spoken."

          "h": "The theme: The four mitzvos of eating on Pesach night corresponding to the Divine Name of Adonut (אדנ״י) and the mouth as the channel of Malchus. The four eating commandments on Seder night—Pesach, Matzah, Maror, and the Four Cups (drinking being subsumed under eating, Pesachim 114b)—correspond numerically to the Name of Adonut (א-ד-נ-י = 65, identical with the acronym of Pesach, Matzah, Maror with the kollel). This is the Divine Name dwelling within Israel, sanctifying their bodily digestion as if \"the Holy One is dwelling within his intestines\" (Ta'anis 11a). This night uniquely reveals the Shechinah through the mouth (\"Malchus is the mouth\", Tikkunei Zohar 17a): the mouth reveals inward thoughts to an outside other via speech, while through eating it elevates lower rungs (vegetative and animal) into human vitality (blood and flesh). Malchus bestows upon subjects and receives from them, for \"there is no king without a nation\" (Kad HaKemach). Creating a dwelling for the Shechinah below is an imperative of the Most High (tzorech gavoha): \"Israel sustains, as it were, their Father in Heaven\" (Zohar III, 7b). More than the calf wishes to suck, the cow yearns to suckle (Pesachim 112a); thus Hashem receives pleasure (nachas ruach) when His will is performed, akin to a dignified man accepting a gift from a woman to betroth her (Kiddushin 7a). While the infinite Essence (Atzmut Ein Sof) transcends all human action, Hashem emanated measured attributes (Middot ha-Ne'etzalot) in the form of Man (Adam d'Atzilus, Yechezkel 1:26; Koheles Rabbah 2:12)—mirrored in the 248 positive and 365 negative mitzvos corresponding to human limbs and sinews (Makkos 23b)—so that mortal man in this world of falsehood may overcome evil and recognize His kingdom."

          "h": "The theme: The final rung of Atzilus manifest as the Shechinah in the hearts of Israel. The final downward rung of the lights of Atzilus is the manifestation of the Shechinah, which is the divine light dwelling within the hearts of the Children of Israel (\"God is the rock of my heart\", Tehillim 73:26; Shir HaShirim Rabbah 5:2). She is designated Knesset Israel—the gathering of all Jewish souls who are an actual portion of Hashem breathed from His innermost spirit. Just as Hashem emanated of His spirit upon the prophets (\"The spirit of Hashem spoke by me\", II Shmuel 23:2; Bamidbar 11:29) so that His light overflowed into the chambers of their hearts to utter \"Thus says Hashem,\" so too this spirit resides within every single Jewish soul. At Mount Sinai all Israel attained prophecy, hearing the first two commandments directly from the Almighty (Makkos 24a); and in the Future He will pour out His spirit upon all flesh (Yoel 3:1). Although in this world this spirit is deeply concealed except among prophets, the essential soul-root of all Israel is emanated from His divine spirit, being the light of His Shechinah dwelling in their innermost hearts as their very vitality."

          "h": "The theme: The emergence of Knesset Israel at the Exodus, the indestructible pillar of faith, and the ultimate repentance of all Jewish souls. The construction of Knesset Israel as an integrated nation began at the Exodus. The Patriarchs had been solitary individuals who recognized the Creator; even regarding Yaakov Avinu, whose bed was unblemished (Pesachim 56a), it had not yet been proven that every one of his descendants—even those submerged in the depths of materialism—possessed an unbreakable root cleaved unto Hashem. This root is faith (emunah): they are \"believers, the children of believers\" (Shabbat 97a), and in the merit of faith they were redeemed from Egypt (Mechilta, Beshalach 6). Habakkuk based the entire Torah upon this single pillar: \"the righteous shall live by his faith\" (Habakkuk 2:4; Makkos 24a), which sustains Israel even in the lowest descent. This faith is planted in every single Jew without exception; even Jewish sinners have sacrificed their lives for the sanctification of the Name (Kiddush Hashem), as expounded on \"the fragrance of his traitors\" (rei'ach bogdav, Bereishis Rabbah 65:22). Even those who apostatized out of spite, upon hearing that Mashiach has arrived, will immediately believe and return; and heretics who ignore the tidings will tremble and repent when the great Shofar is sounded (Yeshayah 27:13), so that \"no outcast shall be expelled from Him\" (II Shmuel 14:14). Unlike gentiles whose root is in evil, Jewish sinners return directly to their ancestral root of pure love for Hashem. The ultimate purpose of Creation is this: that mortals living in the lowest corporeal realm, surrounded by darkness, should recognize His kingdom and sanctify His Name, bringing greater glory to Hashem than thousands of ministering angels."

          "h": "The theme: The election of Yaakov's seed, the descent into the fiftieth gate of impurity in Egypt, and the breakthrough of simple faith (Emunah). Before Yaakov Avinu, only isolated individuals in each generation recognized the divine presence. With Yaakov—whose bed was unblemished—his entire seed was chosen, yet this election required testing in the crucible of Egypt, where Israel sank to the nadir of degradation (\"a nation from the midst of another nation\", Devarim 4:34). Moshe feared they would not believe him (Shemos 4:1) because they had reached the fiftieth gate of impurity (Sha'ar Ha-Nun), where a branch appears severed from its tree. The fiftieth gate mirrors the Jubilee year (Yovel): even the pierced Hebrew slave (eved nirtza) who refused to leave must go free against his will; so too, at Sinai Hashem suspended the mountain like a barrel (kafah aleihem har k'gigis, Shabbat 88a), demonstrating that Israel is eternally bound to Him. Hashem rebuked Moshe for doubting them: Israel are \"believers, the children of believers\" (Shabbat 97a), and in their deepest heart they never lost faith that \"I am Hashem Who dwells with them in the midst of their uncleanness\" (Vayikra 16:16). Recognizing that Hashem is with them even in the valley of the shadow of death (Tehillim 23:4; 139:8) allows the light to dawn from within the darkness, unlocking their speech to chant Hallel so powerfully that it pierced the roofs (hallel paka igara, Pesachim 85b)."

          "h": "The theme: The throat (simanim), eating as a sacred offering, and the Hallel that pierces the roof (paka igara). The Name of Adonut signifies Hashem's sovereign indwelling below, revealed through eating the Korban Pesach. The windpipe (kaneh) and esophagus (veshes) are adjacent organs forming the \"signs\" (simanim) of physical vitality: the windpipe breathes the spirit and articulates speech, while the esophagus ingests food. For an Israelite, physical vitality is sustained not by bread alone, but by \"every word that proceeds out of the mouth of Hashem\" (Devarim 8:3). When food is consumed with pure intent for Heaven—sustaining the soul created by Hashem (Ta'anis 22b; Chullin 7a)—the table resembles the Altar (Chagigah 27a), excelling an altar of physical stones. On weekdays food is sanctified by the blessing; on Shabbat and Yom Tov eating is an explicit mitzvah of delight (oneg); and on Pesach night eating the Korban Pesach and Matzah is an absolute obligation where the physical substance itself is holy, mirroring the priests eating sacrificial offerings (Kohanim ochlim u-ve'alim miskaprim, Pesachim 59b). Through this, the internal organs are sanctified like the Holy of Holies, the blood carries vitality to the heart, and the mouth bursts into Hallel that \"pierces the roof\" (paka igara). The word \"roof\" (gag, ג-ג) represents arrogance and height, from which the name of Gog is derived; an ordinary roof does not elevate itself higher than its construction and lacks the letter Vav (the spirit of life), whereas Gog inflates himself with the Vav (ג-ו-ג) to rise against Hashem and His anointed."

        {
          "h": "The theme: Arrogance as the root of cosmic evil, holy pride versus unholy pride, and piercing the roof (peki'at igara). Arrogance (ga'avah) is the primordial root of all cosmic evil, originating from the shattering of the primordial kings (melachin kadma'in d'mitu, Zohar I, 24b) where each declared \"I shall reign\" (ana emloch). The entire creation began through the arousal of Malchus, for \"there is no king without a nation.\" Planted within man, this drive forms the root of the yetzer tov: desiring to cleave unto Hashem, imitate His ways (Shabbat 133b), and be called by His Name (Bava Batra 75b). This is \"pride in a mitzvah\": \"conduct your presidency with haughty dignity\" (Kesubos 103b) and \"his heart was lifted up in the ways of Hashem\" (II Divrei HaYamim 17:6). Without holy pride, a person falls into spiritual despair (\"By slothfulness the rafters sink in\", Koheles 10:18), imagining his deeds are worthless. To counter this, one must know he is an actual portion of Hashem from Above, declaring: \"When will my deeds reach the deeds of my fathers?\" (Tanna D'vei Eliyahu Rabbah, ch. 25). Conversely, the yetzer hara perverts this into unholy pride: \"you shall be as gods\" (Bereishis 3:5), seeking independence from the Creator. Piercing the roof (peki'at igara) is the nullification of this unholy pride, which forms the dividing wall between Israel and Hashem. For Israel, evil is merely an external husk around the fruit; unlike the nations whose corruption begins in pride, Israel’s stumbling begins in lust, which subsequently drags them into pride. While an ordinary roof is raised only as high as man builds it, Gog possesses an innate Vav (ג-ו-ג) of essential haughtiness extending from beginning to end; his war will erupt at the End of Days, when Israel achieves the final purification of pride through Mashiach."

          "h": "\nThe theme: The slaying of Mashiach ben Yosef, the mutual accusations of Yosef and his brethren, and the descent into Egypt as the purification of desire. Mashiach ben Yosef will be slain in the end-time battle against Gog (Sukkah 52b) because within Yosef lay a subtle root of pride, sensed by his brothers when they asked: \"Shall you indeed reign over us?\" (Bereishis 37:8). This subtle root later branched into the blatant idolatry of his royal descendants Jeroboam and Ahab, who married off Israel to the Baalim (Bereishis Rabbah 84:10). This flaw gives Gog temporary power over Mashiach ben Yosef, whereas Mashiach ben David triumphs over Gog because David embodies consummate humility, remaining \"small\" (ha-katan, I Shmuel 17:14) even upon the throne. Through David, death is swallowed up forever (Yeshayah 25:8) and Mashiach ben Yosef is revived, clarifying that Yosef's pride was directed solely against the heathen nations (Egypt). The sale of Yosef precipitated the Egyptian exile: pagan nations cannot burn the Torah or defile the Temple until Israel does so first through internal strife; when the brothers accused Yosef of pride and he accused them of carnal lust, their mutual recriminations provoked a prosecution on High. Accusations rebound upon the accuser (as when Yeshayahu declared \"I dwell in the midst of a people of unclean lips\" and his mouth was seared with a burning coal, Yeshayahu 6:5–6; Tanchuma, Vayishlach 2). To break Yosef's perceived pride, they sold him into slavery; yet slavery is the archetype of sexual license (Kiddushin 22b; Pesachim 113b). Because Israel's essential purification must proceed from bottom to top—from bodily lust to intellectual pride—Israel was exiled into the depravity of Egypt, where they guarded the covenant of circumcision and achieved the first stage of national purification."

        {
          "h": "\nThe theme: The Exodus as the purification of lust, the roasted meat of kings, and the ten plagues rectifying the stature of evil. The Exodus marks the beginning of Israel's purification from physical lust—the root of Adam's sin which culminated in the physical eating of the forbidden fruit. Hence, their first commandment was an eating mitzvah: eating meat, \"meat of desire\" (b'sar ta'avah), the peak of human craving (\"there is no rejoicing except with meat\", Pesachim 109a). Eating roasted meat (tzali) is the banquet of kings (Chullin 132b), which for Israel was transformed into a mitzvah. The ten plagues in Egypt were ten purifications, proving that Israel was clean of the full stature of evil. The structure of evil begins at the top with pride (its crown) and terminates at the bottom with lust (the feminine / nukva). The first plague, turning their waters to blood, smote rampant lust (water) extending into animal blood; the final plague, the slaying of the firstborn, smote the haughtiness of pride (the firstborn who self-exalt). On the night of Passover, all ten crowns of impurity were smitten. Yet, because Israel's purification from pride was not yet complete (reserved for the Messianic era), they required the blood of the Passover offering upon their doorposts to protect the houses (ha-batim, the surrounding environment). Surrendering the blood (animal life) to Hashem protected their tents, permitting them to eat the Korban Pesach in holy desire, while all uncircumcised males were barred. Through this, speech was rectified and the roof was pierced (paka igara), nullifying the crown of evil at the Seder table."

          "h": "\nThe theme: The four letters of the Name Adonut (אדנ״י), Matzah as the \"bread of poverty\" (lechem oni), and the medicine of healing (meichla d'asvata). The Central Pillar comprises four Sefirot: Keser, Tiferes, Yesod, Malchus, corresponding to the four letters of the Name of Adonut (א-ד-נ-י) and the four eating mitzvos of Seder night. The Korban Pesach corresponds to the letter Aleph (Keser), where holiness penetrates to the root to pierce the roof (paka igara). Today, lacking the sacrifice, \"we render the calves of our lips\" (Hoshea 14:3): the Haggadah and Hallel pierce the intervening screen because Hashem combines good intention with deed (Shabbat 63a). Matzah corresponds to the letter Dalet (dalus, poverty), reflecting Tiferes—the torso of the Shechinah and Knesset Israel, who are poor and destitute (dal v'ani, Bereishis Rabbah 71:1) like the moon which has no light of its own. Matzah is the antithesis of Chametz (the leaven that inflates the dough with arrogance). Matzah is the \"food of healing\" (meichla d'asvata, Zohar II, 183b); as long as a patient undergoes treatment, the harmful pathogen must be completely excluded, wherefore Chametz is banished during the seven days of Passover. The redemption occurred in haste (b'chipazon) because the revelation of divine light in this world is momentary before returning to concealment."

          "h": "The theme: The letter Nun of Adonut (אדנ״י), the mystery of Maror, and the rectification of the feminine fall. The letter Nun of the Name of Adonut corresponds to Yesod d'Nukva (the foundation of the feminine) and the \"feminine waters\" (mayin nukvin), which is the cosmic locus of passion and falling (nefilah). For this reason, the letter Nun is omitted from the alphabetical psalm Tehillah L'David (Tehillim 145), compensated by the letter Samech: \"Hashem supports all that fall (somech l'khol ha-noflim)\" (Berachos 4b), teaching that although the virgin of Israel fell, she will never fall again. This falling is commemorated by eating Maror (bitter herbs), named because the Egyptians embittered their lives (mararu, Shemos 1:14). This bitterness was designed to arouse the soul to raise the virgin of Israel from her spiritual fall. The Korban Pesach was eaten \"with unleavened bread and bitter herbs\" (Shemos 12:8), for through the supreme holiness of the primal root, all aspects—even bitterness and former descents—are elevated and sanctified."

          "h": "The theme: Bitterness as soul-food, the letter Yud of Adonut as the Oral Torah, and the four cups of wine. The preceding bitterness is itself transformed into food and sustenance for the soul, bestowing full vitality, just as the letter Nun is an integral part of the holy Name of Adonut (אדנ״י). In holiness, this feminine desire is consummate sacred fire, but in this world it can lead to spiritual falls, producing bitterness; yet out of this bitterness comes the supreme redemption. The root of the Name consists of the first three letters Aleph-Dalet-Nun (אדון, Master), which Avraham Avinu first revealed (\"until Avraham came and called Him Master\", Berachos 7b). The concluding letter Yud was added to complete the Name as Adonai (אדנ״י), representing the actualization of Malchus in Knesset Israel, who recognize that there is an ultimate Master. This corresponds to the lower wisdom (Chochmah Tata'ah) in the hearts of Israel—the wisdom of the Oral Torah (Torah she-b'al Peh). Parallel to this, the Sages instituted the Four Cups of wine. The Torah commands eating, whereas the Sages added drinking wine (reflecting the opinion in Sanhedrin 70a that the Tree of Knowledge was a grapevine), which represents heightened desire. Wine intoxicated Noach and caused the exile of the Ten Tribes (Bereishis Rabbah 36:4); yet in Israel, wine gladdens the heart and sharpens wisdom (\"wine and fragrance make one wise\", Yoma 76b), for Israel drinks solely to rejoice in Hashem's service. Through holy wine, the lungs draw the liquid, and joy enters the windpipe (kaneh), opening the mouth to sing Hallel (\"song is uttered only over wine\", Berachos 35a), completing the stature of the Shechinah through the final Yud."

          "h": "The theme: The Four Cups as the Four Expressions of Redemption, the judgments on Egypt, and the mystery of the Fourth Cup. The Four Cups correspond to the four expressions of redemption (Shemos 6:6–7) and the four letters of Adonut (אדנ״י). The first three cups reflect the primary redemption from Egypt: Hotzeiti (\"I will bring you out\") is the First Cup of Kiddush, rooted in supernal holiness (Keser / Aleph); Hitzalti (\"I will deliver you\") is the Second Cup after Maggid, reflecting Israel's poverty of deeds (Dalet / Tiferes); Ga'alti (\"I will redeem you\") is the Third Cup over Birkat Hamazon, reflecting complete redemption through an outstretched arm and great judgments (Nun / Yesod). These judgments were \"great\" (shefatim gedolim) because they flowed from the boundless Chesed shown to Israel, for as Israel’s elevation grew, so did the downfall of Egypt (\"if this one is full, that one is desolate\", Megillah 6a). The fourth expression, Lakarta (\"and I will take you to Me for a people\"), corresponds to the final Yud of Adonut—the ultimate goal of Knesset Israel becoming Hashem's nation, crowned through humility (\"what wisdom made a crown for her head, humility made a heel for her sandal\", Yerushalmi Shabbat 1:3). True wisdom is the fear of sin that precedes intellect. The Oral Torah is Hashem's secret (mistorin) entrusted to Israel alone (Sod Hashem lirei'av, Tehillim 25:14). On Seder night each Jew declares in Echad Mi Yode'a: \"One—I know\" (Echad Ani Yode'a), tapping into the divine Ani of the Shechinah within him. The impoverished Dalet receives the Yud and is transformed into the fertile Hei. Over the Fourth Cup, following Hallel, the soul receives new joy after descending into dust, uniting holy fear and joy (Tanna D'vei Eliyahu Rabbah, ch. 3); then one may drink no more (ein maftirin achar ha-pesach afikoman), for he has attained the fullness of the Holy Spirit."

        {
          "h": "The theme: The optional Fifth Cup (Kos Chamishi), the sustenance of the redeemed, and the five rungs of the soul. The optional Fifth Cup (Gevurot Hashem, ch. 65) corresponds to the sustenance (parnasah) that follows redemption. After life is redeemed, it must be sustained through nourishment, as reflected in Hallel HaGadol: after reciting \"Who redeemed us from our adversaries,\" we declare \"Who gives food to all flesh, for His mercy endures forever\" (Tehillim 136:24–25). \"He Who gives life gives sustenance\" (Ta'anis 8b); livelihood is disrupted only through sin (Kiddushin 82b), requiring repentance. The Fifth Cup corresponds to the fifth level of the soul: Nefesh, Ruach, Neshamah, Chayah, and Yechidah. While the lower three expand within the body, Chayah and Yechidah stand as surrounding lights (or makif). In the place of the penitent, the soul cleaves to the Yechidah—the transcendent Ayin which is Israel's Mazal, channeling sustenance unto all flesh, even the lowliest (hinted in Basar / בשר, acronym of bushah, seruchah, rimah / shame, foulness, worms, Sotah 5a). Repentance (teshuvah, sharing the letters of boshet / shame) restores flesh like that of a pure child. In the wilderness, manna was the spiritual sustenance of the letters of the Torah; in the Future, the land of Israel will produce ready-made rolls and fine garments (Shabbat 30b), and physical want will cease. The Fifth Cup remains optional (reshut) because according to pristine creation man does not need to sin and repent; yet mortal man, acknowledging that the unholy yeast and exile still encompass his heart, drinks the Fifth Cup to expand the hidden root of life, broadening the heart through holy awe and joy (\"your heart shall fear and be enlarged\", Yeshayah 60:5), drawing down divine sustenance following redemption."

        {
          "h": "\nThe theme: The bread from heaven, the taste of Manna in Matzah, and the transition from the Written Torah to the Oral Torah. The Mechilta expounds: \"The Torah was given only to those who ate the Manna\" (Mechilta, Beshalach 17). Yet the Torah is an inheritance for the entire congregation of Jacob, as the simple Jew told Rabbi Yannai: \"My inheritance is with you\" (Vayikra Rabbah 9:3). Hence, all Israel are eaters of Manna: the dough taken out of Egypt contained the taste of Manna, and every Matzah eaten on Pesach possesses that selfsame heavenly taste. On Pesach the world is judged for grain (Rosh Hashanah 16a); through eating this \"bread of poverty\" (lechem oni) acknowledging our utter dependence on Hashem, divine sustenance is drawn down for the entire year unto all flesh (\"Who gives food to all flesh, for His mercy endures forever\", Tehillim 136:25). The Psalm then concludes: \"Give thanks unto the God of heaven, for His mercy endures forever\" (ibid. 136:26), because bread hewn from the earth is transformed into bread from heaven. The 26 verses of Ki l'olam chasdo correspond to the 26 generations prior to Sinai sustained by unearned grace; yet at Sinai, Hashem revealed Anochi Havayah. In the wilderness, Manna was the explicit, miraculous bread of the Written Torah; in all subsequent generations, earthly bread earned through labor is recognized as divine sustenance, becoming bread from heaven through the expansion of the Oral Torah (Torah she-b'al Peh / Chochmah Tata'ah), elevating physical earthliness to become pure as the body of heaven."

          "h": "\nThe theme: The opening of Sefer Yehoshua, the cessation of Manna, and the holy contraction of \"bread of poverty\" (lechem oni). The Book of Yehoshua—the first biblical book recorded by human hand after the Chumash—opens with the letter Vav (Va-yehi, Yehoshua 1:1), the letter of truth, and with the word Va-yehi, which everywhere signals distress (Megillah 10b). Upon Moshe's passing, the explicit light of the Written Torah ceased, and forgetfulness entered the world (Temurah 16a), forming the necessary darkness preceding the dawn of the Oral Torah (\"a person does not master words of Torah unless he first stumbles in them\", Gittin 43a). Until the sixteenth of Nissan, Israel subsisted on the leftover Manna in their vessels (Kiddushin 38a); when they ate the produce of the Land, the Manna ceased, inaugurating the lunar light of Yehoshua. This shift was grounded in the Matzah eaten on the fifteenth—the \"bread of poverty.\" While lechem oni implies contraction (tzimtzum), this contraction applies exclusively to hedonistic gluttony (\"the belly of the wicked shall want\", Mishlei 13:25). It does not deprive man of his legitimate bodily needs, for \"the righteous eats to the satisfying of his soul\" (Mishlei 13:25). King Shlomo prayed: \"give me neither poverty nor riches; feed me with the bread of my allotted portion\" (lechem chuki, Mishlei 30:8), each person according to his unique station, like the pauper who required fattened chicken and aged wine (Kesubos 67b). So too with the Manna: \"they gathered each man according to his eating\" (Shemos 16:18), neither exceeding nor lacking."

          "h": "\nThe theme: The expansion within contraction (\"eats a little and it is blessed in his intestines\"), the individualized Omer, and Sefirat HaOmer. This sacred contraction contains immense expansiveness: \"one eats a little and it is blessed in his intestines\" (ochel kima u-misbarech b'me'av, Rashi on Vayikra 26:26). This blessing is qualitative rather than quantitative: bodily pleasure of the palate during eating is restrained, while the influx of vitality into the body and soul through the intestines is richly blessed. The Omer measure (an issaron, a tenth of an ephah) is objectively fixed by standard thumb-breadths for the universal law of the Torah (Eruvin 83b), yet subjectively every single soul gathered and tasted the Manna according to its personal capacity. The Omer offering brought on the sixteenth of Nissan prior to permitting the new grain sweetens the \"bread of poverty\": it declares that holy restraint is not destitution, but the channel for Hashem's blessing that enriches (\"the blessing of Hashem, it makes rich\", Mishlei 10:22), turning the bread of the earth into the bread of heaven. Immediately on that night, Israel begins Sefirat HaOmer—counting from the putting of the sickle to the standing grain (Devarim 16:9), recognizing that all sustenance derives from Hashem. Day by day, the soul is refined through the seven weeks (seven times seven, forty-nine days), culminating on the fiftieth day in the Giving of the Torah from heaven, where earth itself is transformed into heaven."

        {
          "h": "The theme: The start of Sefirat HaOmer, contraction versus expansiveness in Seder foods, and the elevation of bodily superfluity through the Fifth Cup. The counting begins immediately at night on the sixteenth of Nissan, preceding the daytime reaping of the Omer. Seder night contains both tzimtzum (contraction, represented by the Matzah of lechem oni) and harchavah (expansion, represented by the roasted meat and the joy of wine). Yet just as sacred meat and wine do not breed unbridled indulgence, so too the \"bread of poverty\" does not produce destitution, but yields lechem chuko—the righteous eating to satisfy his soul (Mishlei 13:25), like David's cup overflowing with 221 logs (Yoma 76a). The stubborn and rebellious son turns to banditry because false worldly wealth ends in rubble and poverty; in contrast, Israel can elevate even bodily superfluity (motarot) into holiness. The Four Cups are rabbinic obligations; drinking beyond them appears like excess. However, reciting the Fifth Cup over Hallel HaGadol and \"Hashem is my Shepherd, I shall not want\" recognizes that all expansiveness is from Hashem (\"all our works You have wrought for us\", Yeshayah 26:12). In mitzvah meals (Shabbat, Yom Tov, and holy sacrifices, where the Temple gates cried: \"enter and fill your belly with holy offerings!\", Pesachim 57a), eating is completely sanctified. All Israel are children of kings (Shabbat 128a), worthy even of King Shlomo's royal banquet; after reciting a blessing acknowledging that \"the earth He has given to the children of men\" (Berachos 35a), all acquisitions and thoughts become holy unto Hashem."

        {
          "h": "The theme: Sefirat HaOmer as the counting of the clean days, and the fusion of Shabbat and Yom Tov into human action. In Parashat Emor, Scripture commands: \"And you shall count unto you from the morrow after the Shabbat... unto the morrow after the seventh Shabbat\" (Vayikra 23:15–16). By oral tradition (Menachos 65b), we know that the first \"Shabbat\" denotes Yom Tov (the first day of Passover) and the second denotes a \"week\"; Scripture deliberately terms Yom Tov \"Shabbat\" to reveal that Sefirat HaOmer mirrors a woman's counting of seven clean days (shiv'ah nekiyim, Zohar III, 97b). On Pesach the flow of defilement ceased, requiring an hefsek taharah prior to counting. Shabbat represents an eternal, permanent sanctity (kevi'a v'kayma) consecrated directly by Hashem without human effort; Yom Tov is sanctified through human initiative (Yisrael mekadshei l'zmanei), but once man sanctifies himself a little below, Heaven sanctifies him greatly from Above (Yoma 39a), wherefore Yom Tov is also called \"Shabbat\" (cessation of labor). Sefirat HaOmer is man's spiritual exertion: like a woman who does not create her physical purity (which ceases naturally) but merely counts and verifies each clean day, so too on the sixteenth of Nissan Israel brings the first harvest of the Omer—the beginning of human agricultural toil—unto Hashem, declaring that all life and sustenance derive from Him. Acknowledging Hashem purges the defilement of forgetfulness and transfers man from the external domain into his Master's domain. The seven weeks represent the seven lower Sefirot, each comprising seven (49 days), channeling the permanent holiness of Shabbat into the active human faculties of the six days of work."

        {
          "h": "The theme: The 49 days as seven complete statures, the \"Shabbats of the weekday\" (Shabbosot d'chol), and the renewal of Shavuot. Each of the seven emotional attributes is a complete stature comprising seven internal rungs (forming 49 days). The seventh day of each week embodies the culmination of that attribute, mirroring Shabbat; the 49th day—the seventh of the seventh—is termed simply \"Shabbat\" because it completes the entire cycle of human effort, turning the sanctification initiated by Israel below into an eternal, fixed sanctity. This is the mystery of the \"Shabbats of the weekday\" (Shabbosot d'chol, Zohar III, 178a), purifying all 49 days to mirror the holy Shabbat. When the counting is complete (temimot), Israel reaches Shavuot, offering a \"new meal-offering\" (minchah chadashah, Vayikra 23:16). While \"there is nothing new under the sun\" (Koheles 1:9), above the sun—within the holy Torah—there is eternal renewal. Every day words of Torah must be as fresh as on the day they were given (Sifrei, Devarim §33; Rashi on Shemos 19:1), like a wife renewed unto her husband (Niddah 31b) or the moon renewed each month (chodesh / chidush). Genuine renewal requires preceding concealment and stumbling (\"a person does not master words of Torah unless he first stumbles in them\", Gittin 43a). Shavuot is named after the counting of the weeks (Chag HaShavuot), reflecting the passionate yearning (cheshek) of counting toward that day like a lover counting the days until meeting his beloved. Israel, who counts by the moon and is destined to be renewed like her (Sanhedrin 42a), consecrates all faculties through the count, meriting to receive the Torah anew every year on that day."

          "h": "The theme: The fiftieth day as part of the count, Torah as an unexpected find (metzi'ah), and the slumber of Shavuot. Scripture commands counting \"unto the morrow after the seventh Shabbat fifty days\" (Vayikra 23:16); the Rosh and Tosafos (Menachos 65b) struggle with whether the fiftieth day is included. In truth, the fiftieth day is part of the count: celebrating Shavuot as a festival (Yom Tov) is itself its counting, embodying the longing from the preceding human awakening (isarusa d'lesata). Although the Torah was given on Shabbat (Shabbat 86b)—the eternal Torah from Heaven being fixed and unmovable like Shabbat—it required the preparation of human awakening and Moshe sanctifying the nation beforehand. So too: \"If a man says: I have toiled and found—believe him\" (Megillah 6b); yet it is called a \"find\" (metzi'ah), and a find comes only when one’s mind is diverted (b'hesech ha-da'as, Sanhedrin 97a). Human exertion alone could never attain the divine wisdom of Torah, but Hashem gives wisdom only to those who passionately desire it (\"He gives wisdom unto the wise\", Daniel 2:21). The counting days are days of holy awe (yirah), ensuring the forty-nine days are complete (temimot). This explains the judgment upon the disciples of Rabbi Akiva who failed to show proper respect to one another, an imperfection in the attribute of Gevurah and awe. On Shavuot, holy joy must be tempered with awe, as taught in Tanna D'vei Eliyahu Rabbah (ch. 3): \"I rejoiced out of my awe, and I awed out of my joy.\" While Israel does not verbally count the fiftieth day because its holiness arrives automatically, the holy impression (reshimu) of the 49 days remains active even in sleep (\"pleasant was the sleep of Atzeret, for the flea did not bite them\", Shir HaShirim Rabbah 1:18; \"I sleep, but my heart wakes\", Shir HaShirim 5:2), keeping their subconscious imagination cleaved unto Torah."
